analysis.title: Weekly Commentary with Professor Jeremy J. Siegel: Tech Weakness Fuels Bond Rally and Value Rotation
key_insights: The Fed meeting last week was largely uneventful. The S&P 500 and the 10-year Treasury yield ended the session almost exactly where they stood before the announcements, and there was virtually no forward guidance.

The Fed is content to wait until December, given uncertainty around the midterm elections, developments in Iran and oil prices. A 50-basis-point increase remains possible if inflation pressures warrant it. A more substantial deterioration in the AI sector and broader markets could change that calculation.

Rotation continues out of AI-related stocks and into value, alongside falling bond yields. The 10-year Treasury yield has fallen from about 5.35% to 4.90%, with further declines accompanying Nasdaq weakness.
Siegel's mechanism: as AI enthusiasm moderates, expectations for economic growth and capital spending adjust, which pushes interest rates down and supports value stocks.

Uncertainty around AI is extraordinarily high, so small changes in sentiment can move stock prices substantially. The Nasdaq is still less than 10% below its all-time high, which Siegel calls a pullback, not a correction. Individual stocks have fallen much more.

Siegel sees parallels to the rotation that began in 2000 (tech weakens, yields fall, value outperforms), but says current valuations are nowhere near the 2000 bubble extremes and he is not forecasting a comparable Nasdaq decline.

A correction is possible if sentiment keeps deteriorating. A genuine bear market would need much stronger evidence of declining AI spending, weaker demand for computing capacity, or a significant reassessment of industry growth prospects. That evidence has not appeared yet.

Prediction markets have shifted substantially toward the Democrats in the midterms. Current probabilities suggest Democrats could win the Senate, potentially 53-47, with a larger majority possible if late momentum continues. Siegel notes these are not certainties.

Siegel expects a Democratic Congress to produce no major legislative change over the next two years. President Trump retains veto power and much of his agenda is already enacted. Gridlock would postpone major policy changes until the 2028 presidential election, which he sees as more consequential for markets.

Political opposition to data centers is growing, including proposals to restrict new construction in Texas. Siegel expects the economic incentives to prevail, since a rejected project will move to a community that welcomes it. He sees the greater risk to construction as whether AI computing demand justifies the spending.

Overall view is constructive with continued AI-sector volatility expected. He reads the current moves as a healthy reassessment of valuations rather than fundamental economic deterioration, and says improving relative performance of value stocks could continue.

sector_views.rationale: Falling bond yields and cooling AI enthusiasm support value. Siegel says the improving relative performance of value is an important development that could continue.
Constructive overall, but he expects continued volatility. The Nasdaq is in a pullback of less than 10% from its high and a bear market would need evidence of declining AI spending.

Siegel says a 50 bp hike remains possible if inflation pressures warrant it. A deeper AI and financial-market deterioration could change that.
Prediction markets have moved toward the Democrats. Siegel expects gridlock rather than major policy change.
